# Your assignment: the bouncing ball

**Make your Prompt 1 chart move.** Draw the ball 12 times, once at the height of each dot. Show each drawing for two frames. That is 12 drawings, 24 frames, one second [on twos](term:on-twos). Draw by hand, in any tool; the steps show Blender.

**First, fix the chart** with the three checks under your Prompt 1 answer. The chart is your plan.

**What good looks like.** These are four sentences to check your own work against, not a score.

1. The ball reads as having weight.
2. The gaps open as the ball falls and close as it rises into the top of the hop.
3. The two [contact](term:contact-frame) drawings are unmistakable: the ball touches the floor, and you can point to both.
4. The hop is lower than the drop, and the ball ends on the floor.

**Hand in** a short video by Sunday night, where your class collects work, if you want feedback. It is optional, and there is never a grade.

**Your week:** the fall one evening, the hop and landing another, and a look back on Sunday. The next two parts walk you through each evening.

{{prompt:plan-week}}

{{deeper}}

**Why plan the evenings now.** People who decide ahead of time exactly when and where they will do something are more likely to do it than people who only intend to. Naming the evening is most of the work (Gollwitzer, 1999; the full reference is at the end of this module).

**Why the ball does not loop.** A real ball loses height with every bounce, as your chart shows. So this ball drops, hops once and stays down. That one second is the whole piece.

**The two rules this course runs on, in full.**

- **AI organizes everything and touches nothing.** The course's scaffolding, references and calendar are organized with AI's help. Every frame you draw is yours alone, and always will be.
- **No grades, and no tests to pass.** Nothing here scores anything.

**This ball comes back.** In Module 2 you redo it with squash and stretch, and the feedback on this one is what you redo it against.
